text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementEvolutionWhat Do Peahens Really Want?A new chapter in evolutionary biology argues that animals’ bright colors and patterns are about more than just sexRPBy Regan Penaluna9:00 AM CST on November 20, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleFirst of all, there was the trick of staying submerged long enough to hear him. My 3-millimeter wetsuit was made of neoprene, a rubber infused with tiny gas bubbles, and I felt as buoyant as a cork. I was off the coast of Mo’orea, a small island in French Polynesia, floating on the deep cerulean-blue sea.I could just make him out in the distance: the faint white outline of pectoral fins and underbelly, a ghostly silhouette of a male humpback whale suspended vertically, nose pointing down to the ocean floor. He was a giant school bus of a creature dwarfed only by the ocean itself, yet whose song commanded the great expanse. His plaintive chant—ascending high notes interrupted with bass staccatos that caused my flippers to vibrate—was amplified by the walls of the barrier reef. I was getting cold, but the pleasure of his song overpowered my numbing limbs. I wanted to keep myself in the presence of beauty for just a moment longer.This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus.To get it in print, join by Nov 30.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
